documents.title: Generative AI Guidance
documents.summary: UWM's Responsible AI guidance lists general guidelines for anyone using GenAI (follow laws, check output, transparency, security, education) and rules for entering data of different risk levels. It sets no course-level rule on student use.
documents.stance_why: The page states university-wide guidelines for using GenAI tools ('should be adhered to') and a commitment to teaching students AI skills, but it says nothing on what students may do in coursework and does not hand the choice to instructors. It allows use under conditions (law, verification, data review), so permit.

units.why: The introduction states the university's commitment to teaching students AI skills ('committed to providing students with the knowledge, skills and experience'), an institution-level purpose statement and not a rule on use, so P56.
units.anchor: providing students with the knowledge, skills and experience necessary to sustain success
units.frag_start: The University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee is committed
units.fit_note: Also carries a career-readiness rationale (P44), but it is framed as the institution's commitment, so P56 chosen.

units.why: The opening says GenAI offers prospects for those who use it 'creatively, responsibly and ethically' but poses 'considerable dangers' without understanding the risks; this weighs benefits and risks before use, so P118.
units.anchor: it also poses considerable dangers for those who venture into the realm of Generative AI
units.frag_start: However, it also poses considerable dangers

units.why: The guidelines are introduced as expected of anyone using GenAI ('should be adhered to'), a general call to ethical and responsible use with no specific content, so P116.
units.anchor: the following guidelines should be adhered to when utilizing Generative AI tools
units.frag_start: As part of the university’s commitment

units.why: 'Do not use the tools in an unethical way or as part of any illegal activity' is a general conduct ban on unethical or illegal AI use, so P74 (compliance with named policies is the next unit, P77).
units.anchor: Do not use the tools in an unethical way or as part of any illegal
units.frag_start: Do not use the tools in an unethical way

units.why: It requires compliance with hosting entities' acceptable use policies and names Universities of Wisconsin policies (Acceptable Use, Data Classification, Privacy), so P77.
units.anchor: Ensure compliance with acceptable use policies of any entity that hosts Generative AI tools.
units.frag_start: Ensure compliance with acceptable use policies

units.why: Those administering GenAI tools 'should keep up to date on relevant changes to laws, regulations and policies', a duty to stay informed, so P102 rather than P77 because the point is keeping up.
units.anchor: you should keep up to date on relevant changes to laws, regulations and policies
units.frag_start: If you are administering Generative AI tools

units.why: Users with acceptable-use questions are sent to the Information Security Office or the Center for Advancing Student Learning, pointing readers to offices for help, so P115.
units.anchor: consult with the Information Security Office or the Center for Advancing Student Learning
units.frag_start: Individuals who use Generative AI platforms should
units.fit_note: Also names offices that answer questions (close to P80), but they are framed as places to consult, not as owners of the policy.

units.why: 'One should always review the output ... to verify that the information provided is correct' says output may be wrong and must be verified, so P31.
units.anchor: One should always review the output from Generative AI tools for potential bias
units.frag_start: One should always review the output

units.why: It states GenAI 'will completely make up citations, quotations, and descriptions', the fact that output can be fabricated; informs, grouped under P31 as the warning side of the verify rule.
units.anchor: will completely make up citations, quotations, and descriptions
units.frag_start: Generative AI can provide misleading, biased

units.why: For those building an AI system, it says to 'be transparent about the AI components' and explain decisions; this is a transparency and documentation duty on built systems, so P98 (P103 is telling users they face an AI).
units.anchor: if you are building an AI system, be transparent about the AI components
units.frag_start: Additionally, if you are building an AI system
units.fit_note: Transparency and explainability of built systems; P98 is nearest, though it does not mention auditing or monitoring.

units.why: It advises 'Providing documentation on the model and training data' to increase transparency, documentation of AI systems, so P98.
units.anchor: Providing documentation on the model and training data
units.frag_start: Providing documentation on the model

units.why: Users building or using AI tools should 'consult with the Information Security Office' on protections for the model, training data and content against unauthorized access, a security control, so P126.
units.anchor: consult with the Information Security Office about security measures that should be in place
units.frag_start: Whether you are looking to utilize AI tools

units.why: 'Research tools to better understand potential biases' tells users to investigate a tool before relying on it, so P117; bias awareness is the object.
units.anchor: Research tools to better understand potential biases that may be present
units.frag_start: Research tools to better understand potential biases

units.why: 'Learn more about prompt engineering so you can better understand how your prompts affect potential outputs' is practical prompting advice, so P93.
units.anchor: Learn more about prompt engineering so you can better understand how your prompts
units.frag_start: Learn more about prompt engineering

units.why: It states 'UWM is legally and ethically obligated to protect individual and institutional data', the reason for the data rules, so P50 (informs).
units.anchor: UWM is legally and ethically obligated to protect individual and institutional data
units.frag_start: UWM is legally and ethically obligated

units.why: It explains tools 'will use the prompts that users input as part of the training data', so inputs may be exposed; this is the P50 fact that AI tools store prompts.
units.anchor: will use the prompts that users input as part of the training data
units.frag_start: Many Generative AI tools will use the prompts

units.why: Users must keep the UW System Data Classification Policy 'in mind when entering data', with distinct rules per level; a data-protection rule, so P50.
units.anchor: UW System Administration Data Classification Policy in mind when entering data
units.frag_start: One should keep the UW System

units.why: Low-risk data use cases 'are approved by UWM IT' for local, private-cloud and public-cloud use; this institutionally approves a data class for use, so P65.
units.anchor: Use cases involving low risk data are approved by UWM IT
units.frag_start: Use cases involving low risk data
units.fit_note: Approves a data class for use rather than reviewing a named tool.

units.why: Medium-risk data use requires contacting infosec and research computing 'to review your use case' and discussing de-identification, review before use, so P65.
units.anchor: contact the information security office
units.frag_start: For use cases involving medium risk data

units.why: High-risk data (PHI, PII) use requires review by infosec and research computing and a decision on de-identification, so P65.
units.anchor: For use cases involving high risk data, including protected health information or personally identifiable information
units.frag_start: For use cases involving high risk data

units.why: Human-subject research data use requires review by the IRB, infosec and research computing; this governs AI in research, so P62 over P65 since the trigger is research data and the IRB.
units.anchor: For use cases involving human-subject research data, contact the Institutional Review Board
units.frag_start: For use cases involving human-subject research data

documents.title: Syllabus Statements: Guiding Student Generative AI Usage in Your Class
documents.summary: CASL gives instructors a checklist and three sample syllabus statements: full use with citation, specific uses, and a prohibition. It also covers citing AI with the prompt and UWS 14 misconduct.
documents.stance_why: The page offers templates 'Allowing the Full Use', 'Allowing Specific AI Use' and 'Prohibiting AI Use' and tells instructors to state expectations themselves, so the decision is handed to instructors and tiers are listed.

units.why: The checklist tells instructors to 'Explicitly state your expectations for student Generative AI use in the syllabus', an AI statement in every syllabus, so P09.
units.anchor: Explicitly state your expectations for student Generative AI use in the syllabus.
units.frag_start: Explicitly state your expectations

units.why: It asks for written expectations on assignments and to 'talk directly with students about your Generative AI policy, sharing examples', which goes beyond listing the rule, so P66.
units.anchor: talk directly with students about your Generative AI policy, sharing examples
units.frag_start: Include written expectations for Generative AI use
units.fit_note: Also requires written expectations on assignments, a P09-like element.

units.why: Instructors, if applicable, must 'provide information on how students are expected to cite Generative AI use'; it concerns telling students the citation rule, so P24.
units.anchor: provide information on how students are expected to cite Generative AI use for assignments
units.frag_start: If applicable, provide information on how students
units.fit_note: Directs instructors to explain citation expectations; the disclosure rule itself binds students.

units.why: The templates offer three named options (full use, specific use, prohibition) from which instructors pick, so P05 over P04 because the options are named categories.
units.anchor: Syllabus Statement Allowing the Full Use of Generative AI by Students
units.frag_start: Syllabus Statement Allowing the Full Use

units.why: The full-use template says 'you may use Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) for assignments with appropriate citations', so AI is allowed by default with citation.
units.anchor: you may use Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) for assignments with appropriate citations
units.frag_start: In this class, you may use Generative Artificial Intelligence

units.why: It admits limits: 'AI-generated messages and media may be biased, inaccurate, incomplete, or generally unreliable', a warning, so P31.
units.anchor: AI-generated messages and media may be biased, inaccurate, incomplete, or generally unreliable.
units.frag_start: AI-generated messages and media may be biased

units.why: 'It is your responsibility to critically evaluate all responses' makes students verify output, so P31.
units.anchor: It is your responsibility to critically evaluate all responses generated
units.frag_start: It is your responsibility to critically evaluate

units.why: 'You must cite Generative AI when it is used' requires disclosure of any use, so P24.
units.anchor: you must cite Generative AI when it is used
units.frag_start: Furthermore, you must cite Generative AI

units.why: 'Taking credit for any work that is not your own original work constitutes academic misconduct' under UWS Chapter 14, classing misuse as misconduct, so P36 (P29 on ownership is the other candidate).
units.anchor: Taking credit for any work that is not your own original work constitutes academic misconduct
units.frag_start: Taking credit for any work that is not your own

units.why: 'All Generative AI use must be cited and include the prompt' requires the prompt in the citation, so P25.
units.anchor: All Generative AI use must be cited and include the prompt
units.frag_start: All Generative AI use must be cited

units.why: The specific-use template permits chat services 'as a tool to aid in your understanding of content', i.e. a tutor for concepts, so P12; the other two uses in the sentence are coded separately.
units.anchor: as a tool to aid in your understanding of content
units.frag_start: In this course, it is permitted to use Generative AI chat services
units.fit_note: The same sentence also permits idea development (P15) and editing drafts (P91), coded as separate units.

units.why: The same sentence permits using chat services 'to develop ideas', i.e. brainstorming, so P15.
units.anchor: to develop ideas
units.frag_start: In this course, it is permitted to use Generative AI chat services

units.why: The same sentence permits using chat services to 'edit drafts of your work', i.e. editing support, so P91.
units.anchor: edit drafts of your work
units.frag_start: In this course, it is permitted to use Generative AI chat services

units.why: The bracketed note says the description may be replaced by 'naming specific activities or assignments that allow Generative AI use', so the instructor decides per activity, P04.
units.anchor: naming specific activities or assignments that allow Generative AI use
units.frag_start: This description may be replaced by

units.why: The prohibition template says 'The use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is not allowed in this class', a default ban, so P01.
units.anchor: The use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is not allowed in this class.
units.frag_start: The use of Generative Artificial Intelligence

units.why: Prohibited uses include assisting 'in part (e.g., generating ideas, brainstorming, summarizing information) or in whole', so even partial help is banned; P19 (not P105) because summarizing is one listed example of assistance with assignments.
units.anchor: Generative AI used to assist in assignment completion in part
units.frag_start: Generative AI used to assist in assignment completion
units.fit_note: Also bans brainstorming and summarizing as assistance (P15 and P105 aspects).

units.why: Such use 'will be considered Academic Misconduct as defined by UWS Chapter 14', classing prohibited AI use as misconduct, so P36.
units.anchor: will be considered Academic Misconduct as defined by UWS Chapter 14
units.frag_start: Generative AI used to assist in assignment completion

units.why: The quoted UWS 14.03(2) lists misconduct such as 'submitting a paper or assignment as one's own work when a part or all ... is the work of another', defining misuse as passing off others' work, so P29.
units.anchor: submitting a paper or assignment as one’s own work when a part or all
units.frag_start: Examples of academic misconduct include
units.fit_note: Defines misconduct (P36 aspect); P29 chosen because the passage is about submitting others' work as one's own.

units.why: 'If you are uncertain ... please discuss this directly with me before submitting coursework' tells students to ask the instructor when unsure, so P10.
units.anchor: please discuss this directly with me before submitting coursework
units.frag_start: If you are uncertain whether you are using

units.why: 'All assignments that use any external source must be credited using a proper citation' requires crediting sources including AI, so P24.
units.anchor: All assignments that use any external source must be credited using a proper citation.
units.frag_start: All assignments that use any external source

units.why: Students are pointed to the library resource or the instructor ('talk with me directly for assistance') for citation help, human help, so P72.
units.anchor: or talk with me directly for assistance
units.frag_start: Please see the resource on using and citing
units.frag_end: talk with me directly for assistance.
units.fit_note: Also points to a library resource (P115).

notes: Coder B. Guidance page has no student-use policy; syllabus page is templates. Topic codes follow the vocabulary used in earlier dry runs because AGENT_BRIEF.md was not found.
